content: Schizophrenia is a severe and complex mental disorder that profoundly affects individuals and their families. It typically begins in early adulthood, though it can occasionally manifest in childhood or later in life. Men are slightly more likely to be diagnosed with schizophrenia than women, and women generally experience a later onset of the condition. The global lifetime prevalence of schizophrenia is approximately 1%, with a median incidence of 15.2 cases per 100,000 people. Alarmingly, nearly half of those diagnosed with schizophrenia do not receive treatment, and 90% of untreated individuals reside in lowand middle-income countries. The economic burden of schizophrenia has been estimated to range from 0.02% to 1.65% of a country's gross domestic product. Schizophrenia disrupts a person’s thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Its hallmark features include positive symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations, negative symptoms like apathy, emotional blunting, reduced speech, social withdrawal, impaired attention, and anhedonia, as well as disorganized thinking and behavior. Catatonic symptoms, such as unusual posturing or mannerisms, may also occur. Cognitive impairments, including difficulties with attention and short-term memory, are core features of the illness and are strongly associated with social and vocational disabilities. Individuals with schizophrenia often face stigma, discrimination, and violations of their human rights. They are more likely to be single, unemployed, and suffer from chronic health conditions such as cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. On average, people with schizophrenia die 14.5 years earlier than the general population. Antipsychotic medications are the cornerstone of schizophrenia treatment, with two-thirds of patients achieving good or intermediate outcomes. However, one-third of patients do not respond adequately to these treatments and experience poor outcomes. Only a small proportion of individuals with schizophrenia achieve full recovery through a combination of medication and psychosocial interventions. Antipsychotics are effective in reducing positive symptoms and preventing relapse, but they are less effective in addressing negative symptoms. These medications are associated with a range of side effects, including extrapyramidal symptoms, movement disorders, sedation, weight gain, and sexual dysfunction, which can negatively impact treatment adherence. Olanzapine, a second-generation antipsychotic, was approved by the FDA in 1996. It is available in several formulations, including oral tablets, oral disintegrating tablets, intramuscular injections, and extended-release injectable suspensions. Common side effects of olanzapine include weight gain, constipation, dry mouth, peripheral edema, dizziness, drowsiness, orthostatic hypotension, akinesia, and anticholinergic and extrapyramidal symptoms. The chemical structure of olanzapine is 2-methyl-4-(4-methyl-1-piperazinyl)-10H-thieno(2,3-b)(1,5)benzodiazepine. The standard oral dosing of olanzapine for schizophrenia ranges from 2.5 mg to 10 mg per day (low dose), 10 mg to 20 mg per day (medium dose), and more than 20 mg per day (high dose). Intramuscular doses of 150 mg to 300 mg every two weeks or 405 mg every four weeks have demonstrated efficacy. Olanzapine exerts its effects by antagonizing several neurotransmitter receptors, including serotonin (5-HT2A, 5-HT2B, 5-HT2C), alpha-1 adrenergic, and histamine H1 receptors. It has weaker antagonistic effects on muscarinic and dopamine D1 receptors. The mean half-life of oral olanzapine is approximately 33 hours, with a range of 21 to 54 hours. Smoking and male gender are associated with higher clearance rates of olanzapine, but these pharmacokinetic variations do not appear to significantly affect efficacy or adverse effects. Olanzapine is widely prescribed for schizophrenia and has been shown to improve quality of life, reduce extrapyramidal symptoms, and achieve higher medication acceptance compared to some other antipsychotics. However, determining the optimal dose to balance efficacy and side effects remains a challenge for clinicians. Evidence suggests that doses of 10 mg/day to 15 mg/day may maximize therapeutic response, particularly in nonsmoking females. While higher doses (30 mg/day to 40 mg/day) have pharmacokinetic profiles similar to 20 mg/day, they may increase the risk of akathisia. Improvements in quality of life are more pronounced at medium (10 mg/day to 20 mg/day) and high doses (more than 20 mg/day) compared to low doses (2.5 mg/day to 10 mg/day). This review aims to consolidate high-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials to better understand the benefits and risks of varying olanzapine doses for schizophrenia. The findings will support evidence-based clinical decision-making and guide future research directions.
